reading.title: Reading mini-test 5: A Saturday at the Market
paragraphs: A. Every Saturday, Dilnoza goes to the big market in her town with her mother. They leave home at seven in the morning because the market is busy after nine. They go by bus, and the ride takes about twenty minutes.

B. First, they buy vegetables and fruit. Dilnoza likes red apples and sweet grapes, but her mother always buys tomatoes and onions first. The prices are lower at the market than in the supermarket, so many families shop there.

C. Next, they visit the bread section. A man called Rustam sells fresh bread from a traditional oven. He starts baking at five o’clock, and by eight the best bread is usually finished. Dilnoza always eats a small piece while it is still hot.

D. At eleven o’clock, they have tea and a snack at a small cafe near the entrance. Then they carry the heavy bags to the bus stop. Dilnoza is tired when she gets home, but she says the market is the best part of her week.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 1: The Rise of the Rooftop Garden
reading.passageTitle: The Rise of the Rooftop Garden
paragraphs: A. In many large cities, the tops of buildings are among the least used spaces. For most of the twentieth century, roofs were treated as simple coverings, designed to keep rain out and little else. In recent decades, however, architects and city planners have begun to see them as an opportunity. Rooftop gardens, once a rare luxury found on a handful of hotels and private homes, are now appearing on schools, hospitals and office blocks around the world.

B. One of the main reasons for this change is heat. Cities are usually warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and tar roofing absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night. One study of a North American city suggested that if all suitable roofs were covered with plants, the average summer temperature in the centre could fall by up to two degrees Celsius. On a single building, a green roof can also reduce the cost of cooling the rooms below, because the layer of soil and plants acts as insulation.

C. Water management is a second benefit. In a city, rain that falls on hard surfaces runs quickly into drains, and during heavy storms the drainage system can be overwhelmed, causing floods. A green roof absorbs part of this rainfall and releases it slowly. Studies in several European countries have suggested that a roof with a soil layer of about ten centimetres can keep around half of the yearly rainfall from reaching the drains at all.

D. Rooftop gardens are not only practical. They also create habitats for wildlife. In cities where parks are small and far apart, insects and birds can use roofs as stepping stones between green areas. Some enthusiasts have gone further and placed beehives on rooftops, and honey produced in the middle of a city is now sold in several markets as a local speciality.

E. There are, however, challenges. A green roof is much heavier than a conventional one, so the building must be strong enough to carry the extra load, especially when the soil is wet. Installation typically costs two to three times as much as a normal roof, and the plants need regular watering and weeding. Yet over time the plant layer protects the waterproof membrane from sunlight and sudden changes in temperature. As a result, a green roof may last around forty years, compared with about twenty for a conventional roof.

F. Governments have started to respond. A few cities now require new large buildings with flat roofs to include vegetation, while others simply offer tax reductions to owners who install green roofs. Critics argue that rules which demand plants may be less effective than rules which set targets for cooling or water retention, leaving builders free to choose the best method for each building.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 6: Why More People Are Cycling to Work
reading.passageTitle: Why More People Are Cycling to Work
paragraphs: A. In many cities, the number of people who cycle to work has grown steadily over the last ten years. Some workers say that the main reason is cost. A monthly bus ticket can be expensive, while a bicycle needs only a small amount of money for repairs.

B. Health is another reason. Doctors recommend at least thirty minutes of exercise a day, and many office workers find it difficult to fit that into a busy schedule. Cycling to work solves the problem, because the journey itself becomes exercise. One survey found that cyclists took fewer days off sick than people who drove.

C. However, cycling is not always easy. In cities without separate bicycle lanes, riders share the road with cars and buses, and many people feel unsafe. Bad weather is also a problem: few people enjoy arriving at the office wet and cold.

D. To help, some companies now provide showers and secure places to keep bicycles. A few offer small payments to employees who cycle. City councils are also building new lanes, although progress is often slow because the work is expensive.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 3: The Return of the Night Train
reading.passageTitle: The Return of the Night Train
paragraphs: A. Thirty years ago, an overnight train journey was a normal way to cross Europe. Then budget airlines arrived. With tickets sometimes costing less than a train sandwich, many routes lost passengers, and railway companies cancelled their night services one after another. By the early 2010s, only a handful of sleeper trains were left on the continent.

B. Recently, the picture has begun to change. Growing concern about climate change has led many travellers to look for ways to reduce their carbon footprint, and some now choose not to fly when an alternative exists. Several governments have responded by supporting new night routes, and passenger numbers on the restored services have often been higher than expected.

C. Night trains have clear advantages. Passengers travel from one city centre to another, avoiding long journeys to and from airports. Tickets are not always cheaper than flights, but travellers save the cost of a hotel room, since they sleep on the train. Emissions per passenger are also much lower than on a plane.

D. There are, however, practical problems. Many sleeper carriages are old and uncomfortable, and few factories still build new ones. International journeys are complicated by technical differences: countries use different power systems and signals, so locomotives and drivers often have to change at the border. In addition, companies must pay fees for using the tracks, and night services compete for space with freight trains.

E. Operators are trying to solve the comfort problem. New sleeper cars offer private cabins with their own washbasins and showers, and some companies have ordered dozens of them. Better design, supporters argue, can turn the night train from a cheap necessity into a pleasant experience.

F. Most analysts do not expect trains to replace aeroplanes on very long routes. But on journeys of up to about twelve hours, a night train can leave in the evening and arrive in the morning, and that makes it a realistic competitor. If more investment follows, the sleeper train may become a permanent part of European travel once again.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 4: Learning a Language as an Adult
reading.passageTitle: Learning a Language as an Adult
paragraphs: A. Many adults believe that it is too late to learn a foreign language. Research suggests otherwise. In the first months of study, adults often learn grammar rules faster than children, because they can use logic and their knowledge of their own language. Children, on the other hand, usually develop a more natural accent. The two groups simply have different strengths.

B. Motivation matters a great deal. Adults who have a clear goal, such as a new job or a plan to move abroad, tend to keep studying even when progress slows. Those who learn only because they feel they should often give up within weeks. Many teachers therefore begin by asking students what exactly they want to do with the language.

C. Method matters too. One study followed two hundred adult learners for a year. Those who began speaking in the first week, even with simple sentences, progressed faster than those who waited until they felt ready. Spaced repetition, in which words are reviewed at increasing intervals, also helped learners remember vocabulary for longer.

D. Adults face barriers that children do not. Most are short of time, and many are afraid of making mistakes in front of others. Classes where a teacher gives regular, friendly feedback can reduce this fear, and learners in such classes are more likely to continue.

E. Finally, there may be wider benefits. Some researchers believe that people who speak two languages show signs of memory decline later in life, but the evidence is not yet conclusive. What is clear is that learners often report greater confidence and new friendships.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 2: The Hidden Work of Sleep
paragraphs: A. For centuries, sleep was seen as a passive state, a kind of switching off that the body needed in order to recover. Modern research has shown the opposite. Brain scans reveal that during the night the brain passes through several cycles, and in some of them it is almost as active as when we are awake. Far from being idle, the sleeping brain is busy with tasks that cannot be done during the day.

B. One of these tasks is memory. During deep sleep the brain replays the events of the day, moving information from short-term memory to long-term storage. In one experiment, two groups of students studied the same list of words. The group that slept after studying remembered considerably more words the next morning than the group that stayed awake. Sleep, it seems, does not just preserve what we learn; it makes it stronger.

C. The body also uses the night to repair itself. Growth hormone is released mostly during deep sleep, helping muscles and tissues to recover. The immune system is active too: people who regularly sleep for fewer than six hours are more likely to catch a cold than those who sleep for eight. Doctors now regard sleep as one of the basic protections for health, alongside food and exercise.

D. Teenagers face a particular problem. During puberty the body clock shifts, so that young people naturally feel sleepy later in the evening and wake later in the morning. Yet most schools begin early. When some schools moved the start of lessons back by one hour, attendance improved, students reported better moods, and the number of road accidents involving young drivers fell.

E. Modern life makes good sleep harder. Artificial light in the evening, and especially the blue light from phones and tablets, delays the release of melatonin, the hormone that tells the body it is time to sleep. Experts advise keeping a regular schedule, sleeping in a dark room and avoiding screens for an hour before bed.

F. However, sleep is not the same for everyone. Most adults need between seven and nine hours, but some people function well on slightly less, and others need more. Sleeping late at weekends can reduce the effects of a short week, but it only partly makes up for lost sleep. Researchers stress that regular, sufficient sleep cannot simply be stored up or caught up later.

reading.title: IELTS Academic Reading — to‘liq mock 1
reading.passageTitle: Reading Passage 1: The Quiet Revolution of the Bicycle
paragraphs: A. Few machines have changed everyday life as quietly as the bicycle. Its story begins in 1817, when the German inventor Karl Drais built a two-wheeled “running machine”. It had no pedals: the rider sat on a wooden frame and pushed against the ground with both feet. Drais hoped it would offer an alternative to the horse, but the machine was heavy, uncomfortable and difficult to steer on rough roads, and interest soon faded.

B. Pedals appeared several decades later, when makers in France attached cranks directly to the front wheel. Because each turn of the pedals produced only one turn of that wheel, designers who wanted more speed simply made the front wheel larger. The result was the high-wheeled machine of the 1870s, later nicknamed the “penny-farthing”. It was fast, but the rider sat high above the ground, and a sudden stop could throw him over the handlebars. Riding it was regarded as a sport for brave young men rather than a practical form of transport.

C. The decisive change came in the 1880s with the so-called safety bicycle. It had two wheels of similar size and a chain that carried power from the pedals to the rear wheel. Gearing meant that speed no longer depended on wheel size, so the rider could sit lower and put a foot on the ground. Soon afterwards, the air-filled tyre, developed by John Boyd Dunlop in 1888, made journeys far smoother than solid rubber had allowed.

D. The social effects were remarkable. In the 1890s, cycling became a craze in Europe and North America. For the first time, many working people could travel several kilometres to a job without paying for a train or keeping a horse. The bicycle also gave women a new independence of movement, and the fashion for long, heavy skirts began to change because they were impractical for riding.

E. During the twentieth century, cars pushed bicycles to the side of many roads, especially in wealthy countries. Yet the machine never disappeared. In several cities, planners have recently built separate lanes and parking for bicycles, arguing that they reduce traffic and improve public health. Today, electric bicycles, which add a small motor to the rider’s own effort, are introducing cycling to people who once thought hills or long distances made it impossible.

A. Most people are familiar with the experience of studying something carefully, only to find a week later that much of it has gone. In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus tried to measure this loss. Using himself as the only subject, he memorised lists of meaningless syllables and tested how many he could recall after different intervals. His results suggested that forgetting is fastest soon after learning and then slows down, a pattern now known as the forgetting curve.

B. Later research has shown that the curve is not fixed. One of the most reliable findings in psychology is the spacing effect: material that is reviewed several times, with gaps between the sessions, is remembered far longer than material studied for the same total time in a single block. Cramming the night before an examination may produce a reasonable score the next morning, but most of what was learned disappears soon afterwards.

C. A second powerful technique is retrieval practice. When learners try to recall information without looking at it — for example, by answering questions or writing down everything they remember — they strengthen the memory more than when they simply reread their notes. Rereading feels productive because the material looks familiar, but familiarity is not the same as being able to produce the information when it is needed.

D. Why should effortful recall be so effective? One explanation is that each successful retrieval makes the route to a memory easier to find next time. Another is that recall shows learners which parts they have not yet mastered, so they can direct their attention there. Interestingly, researchers have found that a failed attempt to remember, if it is followed by the correct answer, can still improve later recall.

E. Sleep also plays an important part. Studies in which people learn new material in the evening and are tested the following morning suggest that a night of sleep helps to stabilise what has been learned. Students who give up sleep to study longer may therefore weaken the very memories they are trying to build.

F. None of these findings is new, yet they are often ignored. Many students continue to highlight, reread and cram, partly because these methods feel easier. Some teachers now build short, low-pressure quizzes into their lessons and return to earlier topics weeks later. The aim is not to test students more, but to turn remembering itself into a way of learning.

A. On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. This difference, called the urban heat island effect, has been observed in cities on every continent. It is usually strongest at night, when the surrounding fields cool quickly while streets and buildings go on releasing the heat they absorbed during the day.

B. Several features of cities produce the effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and roofs absorb a large share of the sunlight that falls on them. Concrete and brick store this heat and release it slowly. In addition, cities have fewer trees and less open soil, so less water evaporates — a process that naturally cools the air. Heat from vehicles, factories and air conditioners adds a further, smaller contribution.

C. The consequences are more than a matter of comfort. During heatwaves, high night-time temperatures prevent the body from recovering, and older people and those with health problems face the greatest risk. Hotter cities also use more electricity for cooling, which can place pressure on power networks at the moments of highest demand.

D. Some solutions are surprisingly simple. Painting roofs in light colours reflects more sunlight back into the sky, and so-called cool pavements use materials that stay cooler under the sun. Trees provide shade and release water vapour through their leaves, and parks of even modest size can be measurably cooler than the streets around them. Green roofs, covered with plants, insulate buildings and absorb rainwater as well as cooling the air.

E. However, none of these measures is a complete answer. Light-coloured surfaces can reflect sunlight onto nearby buildings and pedestrians, and trees need water, space and years of care before they offer much shade. In dry regions, planners must balance the cooling benefits of vegetation against the limited supply of water. Experts therefore tend to recommend a combination of measures chosen to suit each neighbourhood.

F. Traditional architecture offers further ideas. In many hot countries, older districts were built with narrow streets that remain in shade for most of the day, thick walls that slow the movement of heat, and inner courtyards with plants or water. Some architects argue that these designs, developed over centuries, deserve as much attention as new technology. As summers become hotter, the question of how to keep cities cool is likely to become one of the central challenges of urban planning.

listening.title: Listening mini-test 2: Library introduction
listening.context: Greenfield Public Library: yangi a’zolar uchun qisqa tanishtiruv (monolog).

script.speaker: A
script.text: Welcome to Greenfield Public Library. I'm going to give you a short introduction before you start exploring.

script.speaker: A
script.text: First, our opening hours. We are open from nine in the morning until eight in the evening, Monday to Friday. On Saturdays we open later, at ten, and close at four. We are closed on Sundays.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Joining the library is free for all residents. To join, you will need to bring proof of address, such as a bank letter or a utility bill. A passport is not enough, because it does not show where you live.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The children's section is on the first floor, next to the cafe. The ground floor has newspapers and the main book collection.

script.speaker: A
script.text: We have twelve public computers. Each session lasts sixty minutes, and you can extend it if nobody is waiting. Printing used to cost fifteen pence a page, but from this month it is ten pence.

script.speaker: A
script.text: If you need somewhere quiet to study, there is a study room on the second floor. You cannot just walk in, though. You must book it at the main desk, and bookings are for two hours.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Books can be borrowed for three weeks. If you return a book late, there is a charge of twenty pence per day. There is also a return box outside the main entrance, which is open twenty-four hours.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Finally, free wireless internet is available throughout the building. The password is readmore, all one word, with no capital letters. Thank you, and enjoy your visit.

listening.context: Tutor va talaba Maria: tadqiqot loyihasi haqida suhbat.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So, Maria, how is your research project going?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Quite well, thank you. I've decided to focus on plastic recycling in our city, rather than the whole country.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. That's more realistic. And what methods are you planning to use?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I was going to send a questionnaire, but a friend suggested interviews, because they would give me more detail.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Interviews take longer, though. How many people are you thinking of?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Fifteen in total. Ten residents and five shop owners.

script.speaker: A
script.text: That sounds manageable. When do you need to finish collecting the data?

script.speaker: B
script.text: By the end of March. Then I'll analyse the results in April.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Remember that the final report must be three thousand words, and the deadline is the twelfth of May.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes. Can I include graphs? Do they count towards the word limit?

script.speaker: A
script.text: No, graphs don't count, but you must label them clearly.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Great. And where can I find statistics on recycling?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The city council website has figures, but check the university library as well. The council data is only updated every two years, so it may be out of date.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thanks. One last thing: my presentation.

script.speaker: A
script.text: It's on the fifth of June. Ten minutes, plus questions, and please use no more than eight slides.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Eight slides. Understood. Thank you very much.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Today I'd like to talk about urban beekeeping. Over the last decade, the number of hives in cities has increased rapidly, and many people are surprised to hear that city bees often produce more honey than bees in the countryside.

script.speaker: A
script.text: There are two main reasons for this. The first is variety. Parks, gardens and even balconies provide flowers throughout the season, whereas farmland may offer a single crop for only a few weeks. The second is temperature. Cities are warmer, so bees can begin collecting food earlier in the spring.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Let me give you some figures. In summer, a typical hive contains around fifty thousand bees. An individual worker bee lives for only about six weeks. In a good location, one hive can produce an average of twenty kilograms of honey a year.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course, there are challenges. Neighbours may worry about stings, so hives in cities are usually placed on rooftops, at least three metres above the ground, or behind a tall fence.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Another problem is competition. If there are too many hives in one area, the bees compete for nectar, and wild bees can suffer. Experts therefore recommend no more than about five hives per square kilometre.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Finally, people sometimes ask whether city honey is safe. It is regularly tested for pollution, and the results show that it is generally safe to eat. Thank you for listening.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good afternoon, Greenway Community Centre. This is Helen speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Hello. I saw a poster about your evening courses, and I'd like to book a place on one of them.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Certainly. Which course are you interested in?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The photography course for beginners. I'm not sure if there are still places.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Let me check. Yes, there are three places left on the Thursday group. The Monday group is already full, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Thursday is fine, actually. Probably better for me.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good. I'll need to take a few details. Could I have your full name, please?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yes, it's Mark Fenwick.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Could you spell the surname?

script.speaker: B
script.text: F, E, N, W, I, C, K.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Thank you. And your address?

script.speaker: B
script.text: It's twenty-seven Mill Lane, in Ashford.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Twenty-seven Mill Lane. And a phone number we can reach you on?

script.speaker: B
script.text: My mobile is oh seven nine six two, four four eight, three one oh.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Oh seven nine six two, four four eight, three one oh. Lovely. Now, the course runs for eight weeks, starting on the ninth of October.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And what time does it start?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Classes begin at half past seven and finish at nine. They're held in Room 12, which is on the first floor, next to the library.

script.speaker: B
script.text: And how much does it cost?

script.speaker: A
script.text: The full price is ninety-five pounds, but if you're a member of the centre, it's seventy.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'm not a member. Is it worth joining?

script.speaker: A
script.text: Membership is fifteen pounds a year, so you would save ten pounds on this course alone, and you'd also get a discount at the café.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Then I'll join. Do I need to bring my own camera?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You can use your phone for the first two weeks. After that, the tutor recommends a simple digital camera, but the centre can lend you one if necessary. You'll also need a notebook.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That sounds fine. How do I pay?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You can pay by card over the phone now, or in cash at reception before the first class.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll pay at reception, if that's all right.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course. Just one more thing: how did you hear about the course?

script.speaker: B
script.text: A friend told me about it, and then I saw the poster at the station.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Wonderful. I'll send you a confirmation by text message today. We look forward to seeing you.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hartley Gardens. My name is Tom, and I'm one of the volunteers here. Before you set off, I'd like to give you a short introduction and a few practical details.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The gardens were created in 1902 by a local doctor, Edward Hartley, who believed that fresh air and plants were good for his patients. After his death, the house was turned into a school for a while, and the gardens were neglected. They were only restored in the 1990s, when a group of local residents raised the money to save them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Today the gardens cover about twelve hectares. If you look at the map you were given, you'll see that the main path goes in a circle. If you follow it all the way round, it takes about an hour and a half, but there are several shorter routes as well.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Let me mention a few of the highlights. Just past the entrance, on your left, is the Rose Garden. It's at its best in June, so you've come at the right time. Beyond that is the lake. Please don't feed the ducks, because bread is actually bad for them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: On the far side of the lake you'll find the glasshouse, which contains tropical plants. It's kept very warm, so you may want to take off your coat before you go in. Next to it is the children's play area, which was rebuilt last year.

script.speaker: B
script.text: One of our newest features is the Sensory Garden, near the north gate. It was designed for visitors with poor eyesight, so all the plants were chosen for their smell or the way they feel when you touch them. Please do touch them; that's what they're there for.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Now, some practical information. The café is in the old stable building, and it's open until five. The toilets are next to the café and also by the main car park. If you need help, our volunteers are wearing green jackets.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Finally, there's a talk by our head gardener at three o'clock this afternoon in the education centre. It's about growing vegetables in small spaces, and it's free, but places are limited, so please collect a ticket from the information desk if you'd like to attend.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's all from me. Enjoy your visit.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Hi, Daniel. Have you got a few minutes to talk about our presentation? It's only two weeks away now.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Sure, Emma. I've been reading about our topic, the four-day working week, and I think we've got plenty of material.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good. I thought we could start with the trial that took place in Britain a few years ago. Most of the companies that took part decided to continue with the shorter week afterwards.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Yes, but I think we should be careful there. The companies chose to take part, so they were probably more enthusiastic than average. That might make the results look better than they would be in general.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That's a good point. We should mention it as a limitation.

script.speaker: D
script.text: What surprised me was that productivity didn't fall in most of the companies. I expected it to drop at least a little.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Me too. Apparently people cut down on long meetings and wasted time. One manager said meetings were reduced to thirty minutes.

script.speaker: D
script.text: And the staff reported less stress and better sleep. Although those results came from questionnaires, so they depend on what people said about themselves.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Right. Now, how should we divide the work? I'd be happy to do the background and the history of working hours.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Then I'll take the results of the trial. And maybe we can both do the conclusion together?

script.speaker: C
script.text: Fine. What about visuals? Our tutor said she wanted fewer slides with words and more charts.

script.speaker: D
script.text: I can make the charts. I'm better with spreadsheets than you are, I think.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That's true! I'll find a short video clip, then. Something from an interview with an employee, maybe. Not more than a minute, though.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Good idea. One thing I'm worried about is the question time at the end. Some people are bound to ask whether this would work in hospitals or schools.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We should prepare an answer to that. The trial was mainly in offices, so we can say the evidence for other sectors is still limited.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Agreed. When shall we practise?

script.speaker: C
script.text: How about next Wednesday afternoon in the library? We could book one of the study rooms.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Wednesday's fine, but the library rooms are always busy. Let's use the empty classroom on the second floor instead.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Perfect. I'll send you my part by Monday so you can read it first.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good morning. Today I'm going to talk about honeybees, and in particular about how they communicate. For a long time, people wondered how bees that had found a good source of food were able to direct other bees to it. The answer came from the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who studied bees for many years and later received a Nobel Prize for his work.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Von Frisch discovered that a bee returning to the hive performs a kind of dance on the surface of the honeycomb. When the food is close to the hive, the bee moves in small circles. This is called the round dance, and it simply tells the other bees that food is nearby.

script.speaker: A
script.text: When the food is further away, the bee performs what is known as the waggle dance. It runs forward in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement. The direction of the straight run shows the direction of the food in relation to the sun, and the length of the waggle tells the other bees the distance they need to fly.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What is remarkable is that the hive is usually dark, so the other bees cannot see the dance clearly. Instead, they follow the dancer closely and pick up the information through touch and vibration. They also learn the smell of the flowers from the dancer's body.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course, not every scientist accepted these findings at first. Some argued that bees simply followed the scent of the food. It was only later, when researchers used radar to track individual bees, that it became clear that the bees really did fly in the direction indicated by the dance.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Why does this matter today? Bees are responsible for pollinating a large proportion of the crops we eat, and in many regions bee populations have declined. Several causes have been suggested, including disease, the loss of wild flowers and the use of certain chemicals on farms.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Understanding how bees communicate can help farmers and planners. For example, if we know how far bees are prepared to fly, we can decide where to plant strips of flowers so that bees can reach them easily. In some cities, people are now encouraged to plant flowers on balconies and roofs.

script.speaker: A
script.text: In our next lecture, we'll look at how bees choose a new home when a colony becomes too large, a process in which, interestingly, the dance also plays a central role.
